opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest reason is that in practice, these things aren't separate problems. They show up in the same system, often in the same interaction.

When we started building generative AI applications, there was a tendency to treat them as different workstreams. You had people measuring quality: is the answer accurate, is it grounded, is it relevant? Then a separate group looked at safety: does it produce harmful content? Then the security folks thought about adversarial attacks like jailbreaks or prompt injection. But the moment you put a real application in front of real users, you see how tangled these are.

Take groundedness. If a model fabricates something in a summary, is that a quality problem or a safety problem? In a medical or legal context, it's both. Prompt injection is a security attack, but what it often does is cause the system to produce harmful content or take an action it shouldn't, which is a safety outcome. So if you measure only one dimension, you end up with blind spots exactly where they overlap.

The second reason is trade-offs. Every mitigation you add has a cost somewhere else. Make the safety system more aggressive and you may start refusing legitimate requests, which hurts quality and the user experience. Tune the model to follow instructions really well and you may make it more susceptible to instructions hidden in a document it retrieves. If you evaluate each dimension in isolation, you can't see those trade-offs, and you end up optimizing one metric while quietly degrading another. Looking at them together gives you a full picture so you can make an informed decision about where the right balance is for your scenario.

The third piece is practical: it's the same workflow. You need a good set of test data representing how people will actually use the system, including the adversarial ways. You need automated evaluation that runs at scale, and you need to rerun it every time you change the prompt, swap the model, or add a new data source. Building that pipeline once and running quality, safety, and robustness through it is far more efficient than three disconnected processes, and it makes evaluation something teams actually do continuously rather than a gate at the end.

And honestly, it's a mindset shift. We want teams to think of responsible AI not as a separate checklist but as part of what it means to build a good product. A system that's helpful but easily manipulated isn't a good system. A system that's perfectly safe but never answers anything useful isn't either. Evaluating them together is how you get to something that's genuinely trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response explains that stronger safety measures can cause legitimate requests to be refused, hurting quality, while instruction-following improvements can increase susceptibility to prompt attacks. It says evaluating dimensions together reveals these trade-offs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. The short answer is that in practice, you can't actually separate them. When we started building responsible AI tooling for generative models, we noticed that teams would treat quality as the "real" work and then bolt safety on at the end as a kind of compliance checkbox. And that approach just breaks down with generative systems, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that these dimensions trade off against each other. If I make a model more cautious so it refuses more harmful requests, I'm almost certainly going to see it over-refuse on perfectly benign ones, and that shows up as a quality regression. If I tune for groundedness so the model sticks closely to my retrieved documents, that can change how it handles edge cases where a user is trying to manipulate it. So if you evaluate these in isolation, you can ship a change that looks like a win on one dashboard and quietly degrades the system on another. You only see the real picture when the metrics sit side by side on the same test runs.

The second reason is that the failure modes blur together. With a classifier, "wrong answer" and "unsafe answer" were pretty distinct categories. With a generative model, a hallucination can be a safety issue. A jailbreak often works precisely by exploiting the model's helpfulness, which is a quality property. So the adversarial robustness question isn't really "can someone break the safety filter," it's "how does the whole system behave under pressure," and that's inseparable from how it behaves normally.

And the third piece is just engineering reality. Teams iterate constantly. They're changing prompts, swapping models, adjusting retrieval. If safety and robustness testing live in a separate process owned by a separate team that runs quarterly, they'll never keep pace. The only way this works is if a developer can make a change, run one evaluation, and see quality, safety, and adversarial results together before they ship. That's what moves responsible AI from a review gate into something that's actually part of how you build.

r001.rationale: It says the dimensions trade off: increasing refusals for safety can cause benign over-refusal and a quality regression, so evaluating them side by side reveals cross-dimension effects.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re deeply connected. A system isn’t really high quality if it gives you a useful answer most of the time but becomes unsafe when someone changes the wording or deliberately tries to push it outside its intended use. And a system that refuses everything might look safe on one metric, but it’s not useful.

So you want to evaluate those dimensions together, because the choices you make affect all three. If you add a safety mitigation, does it actually hold up under adversarial testing? Does it also cause the system to refuse legitimate requests? If you improve the model’s ability to follow instructions, does that make it better at following malicious instructions, too?

The goal is to understand the behavior of the whole system in the context where you’re deploying it. You need realistic tasks, safety tests, and attempts to break the system, and then you need to use those results together to decide what to improve. Otherwise, you can optimize one metric and miss a problem that really matters to the people using it.

r001.rationale: The response explains that safety mitigations and instruction-following improvements can affect adversarial robustness and legitimate-usefulness, so evaluating all three dimensions together reveals trade-offs and regressions.

sol-6.1.text:
Because they’re all dimensions of whether the system actually works for the people using it. A model can give a very fluent answer that’s wrong or harmful. And you can make a system appear safer by having it refuse almost everything, but then it’s not useful. So you really need to understand those tradeoffs together.

Adversarial testing adds another perspective: does the behavior you measured hold up when someone deliberately tries to push the system outside its intended boundaries? You might have great results on typical requests, but a small change in how a request is phrased can expose a failure.

I think the key is to evaluate the whole application in its actual context—the model, the instructions, the data it retrieves, and any tools it can use. Then, as you improve a safety mitigation, you also check whether you’ve hurt quality or introduced a new vulnerability. That gives teams a much more meaningful picture of whether the system is ready to deploy.

r001.rationale: The response says the dimensions involve trade-offs, giving the example that improving a safety mitigation may hurt quality or introduce a vulnerability.
